title: Amen (CCC 1061–1065)
hook: the Creed ends as scripture does: Amen, Christ himself is the Amen

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new heaven and earth: creation renewed, not thrown away. Your line was all things new. Did you get to that one small thing for the earth? Today, the last word of the Creed. Day one thousand eighty-six.

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." That's the last verse of the Bible in the Douay-Rheims, and its last word is the one the Creed ends on too. The Creed opens with I believe and travels a long way: God, Christ, the Spirit, the Church, forgiveness, the resurrection, life everlasting. Then a whole church closes it with that same small word. For days now, this path has walked through the first part of the Catechism, the part about what Catholics believe. The Catechism closes that part the way the Creed does, by stopping on that one word.
screen: `THE BIBLE'S LAST WORD.` → `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. The Catechism explains that in Hebrew, amen shares its root with the word for believing. It carries the sense of something solid, trustworthy, faithful, something you can lean your weight on. So saying amen isn't just saying I agree. It's saying this holds. Second, God first. The Catechism points out that in the prophet Isaiah, God himself is called the God of truth, which in Hebrew is the God of amen. People can say amen to God's promises because God is faithful first. Third, a bookend. The Creed's last word, the Catechism says, repeats and confirms its first: I believe. The whole prayer sits between them, like a book between two covers. It quotes Saint Augustine, who told new Christians to let the Creed be a kind of mirror, something to look into every day and see whether they still believe what they say. Fourth, and most surprising, the Amen has a name. In the Apocalypse, Christ speaks to a church and introduces himself like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." Not someone who says amen. The Amen. Saint Paul writes that all God's promises find their yes in Christ. In Catholic belief, Christ is God's final and faithful yes to the world, and when people say amen, they're joining their small yes to his. So the word at the end of the Creed isn't a full stop. For Catholics, it's a signature: everything above this line, I'm leaning my weight on it.
screen: `SOLID, TRUSTWORTHY, FAITHFUL.` · `THE GOD OF AMEN.` · `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` · `THESE THINGS SAITH THE AMEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say amen slowly. Settle, and breathe. Let your breath go in, and on the way out, say the word quietly, or just in your head, stretched long: amen. Then do it again, and this time let it mean what the Catechism says it means: this holds. If you pray, you can say it to God about something you trust him with. If you don't pray, you can let it be a yes to something true in your life: a person, a promise, a place that has held you up. Keep coming back to the word, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Amen. A Hebrew word for what is solid and faithful, the last word of the Creed, and, in the Apocalypse, a name for Christ himself. Today's word.
Your line: so be it. The next time you say amen, or hear it, or say yes to anything today, slow down and mean it. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics say amen at the end of the Creed, after prayers at Mass, and when receiving Communion, when the minister says "the Body of Christ" and each person answers amen.
